chapter_theme: Renunciation is the removal of attachment to what is 'mine' and even to the 'I'. It begins with freedom from each thing's pain and reaches release, while those who keep any hold stay in the net. The chapter ends in the paradox that one must cling to get free of clinging.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: giving up the outer attachment 'mine' (341-344), giving up the inner attachment 'I', that is, the body (345), release for those who give up both (346), both outcomes (347-349), and the means (350).

341.reading: From whatever, whatever one has left, from that, from that, one has no pain.
341.nuance: The doubled words make this piecemeal, and Parimelazhagar accepts that: giving up everything at once is best, but each thing left removes its own pain. So renunciation isn't all or nothing in this verse.

342.reading: If you want it, renounce while there is time; after renouncing, there are many things that come about here.
342.nuance: The verse is elliptical. Parimelazhagar concedes that he has supplied both 'joys' and 'time', so much of what appears to be said is commentary. Its surprise, on his reading, is that renunciation brings joys in this life and not only the end of pain. It also starts with வேண்டின், 'if you want'.

positions.position: Renounce in time, while young, so as to have these joys for longer.
positions.quote: அவ் இன்பங்களை வேண்டின், அவற்றைக் காலம் பெறத் துறக்க.

positions.position: Renounce if you want gain for your own soul.
Renounce while everything is still there to give up.
positions.quote: எல்லாம் இருக்கும் போதே அவற்றைத் துறந்து விடுவானே யானால்,

343.reading: The domain of the five must be crushed, and all that one has wanted must be let go at once.
343.nuance: புலம் is the field of the senses, their enjoyment, and not the organs that Pope's gloss has destroyed. Parimelazhagar gives the reason for 'at once': sense enjoyment fed with objects only burns higher, like fire with fuel.

344.reading: Having nothing at all is natural to austerity; having anything brings back confusion all over again.
344.nuance: Parimelazhagar's reading is psychological: keep one thing and everything given up returns through it. Manakkudavar links the confusion to further birth.

345.reading: For those set on cutting off births, even the body is excess; why then any further ties?
345.nuance: The body is the one tool needed for the work and still counts as excess. Parimelazhagar divides it into gross and subtle bodies, a doctrine the verse doesn't state, and makes this the renunciation of the inner 'I'.

346.reading: One who cuts off the pride of saying 'I' and 'mine' enters a world higher than the gods'.
346.nuance: செருக்கு is glossed as delusion by the older commentators, as Parimelazhagar also does at 201: for them, the problem is a false identification and not arrogant manners. The body isn't 'I' and goods aren't 'mine'.

positions.position: This is the world of release, beyond even the gods' reach.
This is earthly fame greater than heaven-high fame.

347.reading: Griefs that hold and won't let go hold those who hold attachment and won't let go.
347.nuance: The two lines use one verb for the person and the griefs, so that the grip one keeps and the grip one suffers are shown to be the same act.

348.reading: Those who have thoroughly renounced have got to the head; the rest, in confusion, are in the net.
348.nuance: தலைப்பட்டார் doesn't say what has been reached, and the past tense suggests it is already done. Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar say release, Kalaignar says a high state, and Pope's gloss has 'absorption into God', which adds a theology the Tamil doesn't have.

349.reading: The moment attachment ends it cuts off births; otherwise impermanence is what is seen.
349.nuance: கண்ணே, 'at the very moment', makes release immediate, as an effect stops with its cause. Parimelazhagar takes மற்று as 'if not', and Pope's couplet and gloss diverge on it, the couplet making impermanence what is seen after the release, the gloss what is seen without it.

350.reading: Cling to the clinging of the one who has no clinging; cling to that clinging, in order to let clinging go.
350.nuance: பற்று comes six times in seven words, and the chapter on letting go ends by commanding a holding on. A useful attachment is the ladder that lets one drop the others.

positions.position: The unattached one is the Lord, and what is held is the path to release that he taught.
positions.quote: எல்லாப் பொருளையும் பற்றி நின்றே பற்றற்ற இறைவன் ஓதிய வீட்டு நெறியை,

positions.position: What is held is a practice: meditative absorption.
The unattached one is any person so unattached, and it is him one should hold to.
positions.quote: எதிலும் பற்றில்லாதவராக யார் இருக்கிறாரோ அவரிடம் மட்டும் பற்றுக் கொள்ள வேண்டும்.

links.note: 341 says each thing given up removes that thing's pain, a piecemeal gain. 344 says keeping even one thing brings it all back. Parimelazhagar accepts both, one as a gain and the other as a risk, but the practical advice differs.

343 demands that the domain of the five senses be crushed. 1101 finds all five senses' delights gathered in the beloved. The third book takes what renunciation would destroy and fulfils it in one person.
இன்மை, having nothing, is natural and right for austerity in 344. In 1041, poverty, the same word, is what nothing else can match for misery. The word changes value completely with who has chosen it.

50 places the good householder among the gods, and 346 and 348 put full renouncers beyond them and everyone else in the net. Parimelazhagar's ladder (fame and heaven for householders, release for renouncers) is how the commentary fits these together.

7 says that only those who join the feet of the incomparable one can be rid of grief. 350 repeats the structure with attachment. Parimelazhagar himself notes that the generic word is kept to match the invocation chapter.

source_issues: 341: no Manakkudavar commentary is aligned to this verse.
